Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- House and Senate Democrats reached agreement late Monday on a budget resolution for 2010, which includes key spending priorities for the young Obama administration. The Senate and House could vote on the budget resolution Tuesday. President Obama's budget request is $3.67 trillion. "This budget is a major accomplishment," Senate Budget Committee Chairman Kent Conrad said in a statement. "We are meeting President Obama's goals of reducing our dependence on foreign energy, striving for excellence in education, reforming our health care system, and providing middle-class tax relief." The agreement came as lawmakers were reconciling the House and Senate versions of the budget package. The president's budget request is $3.67 trillion. The full Senate and House are each expected to vote on the fiscal 2010 budget resolution this week. The House vote could come as soon as Tuesday. Budget negotiators have fast-tracked part of the budget process. Major health reform is likely to pass this year, because the special process -- known as budget reconciliation -- won't allow Republicans to filibuster the legislation, as was widely expected. Democrats, who currently control 58 seats in the Senate, will be able to pass it with a simple majority vote, instead of the 60 needed to overcome a filibuster. Separately, conservative Democrats in the House, who have been pushing for a strong statement from leadership on fiscal responsibility in the budget, may have some of their concerns addressed. A Democratic aide told CNN that House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and House Majority Whip Steny Hoyer are drafting a letter to Senate leaders "throwing down the gauntlet" to insist that a pay-as-you-go system be followed, which would require new federal spending to be offset with budget cuts or tax increases. President Barack Obama called for the so-called "PAYGO" legislation in his weekend radio address. The budget resolution would limit increases in non-defense discretionary spending to 2.9 percent through 2014, according to Conrad. "While the budget resolution takes important steps in the near-term of cutting the deficit in half by 2012 and by two-thirds by 2014, it is clear that more will be needed to address the long-term fiscal imbalance confronting the nation beyond the five-year budget window," said Conrad. President Obama gathered his Cabinet members last week and challenged them to cut a total of $100 million in the next 90 days. In the context of the federal budget, $100 million in savings is a tiny amount, critics said. It is the equivalent, according to one example, of having a car dealer offer to shave $1 from the cost of a $36,700 vehicle. "Any amount of savings is obviously welcome," Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Kentucky, said at the time. "But ($100 million is) about the average amount we'll spend every single day just covering the interest on the stimulus package that we passed earlier this year." White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs said ordinary Americans would nevertheless appreciate the savings effort. "Only in Washington, D.C., is $100 million dollars not a lot of money. It is where I'm from. It is where I grew up. And I think it is for hundreds of millions of Americans." CNN's Deirdre Walsh contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Late Monday, Democratic negotiators from the House and Senate finalized a compromise fiscal 2010 budget resolution that reflects major spending objectives of the new Obama administration.

Both chambers could begin voting on the resolution Tuesday, although votes are expected sometime this week. The House, in particular, may act as early as Tuesday. President Obama has proposed a $3.67 trillion budget.

Senate Budget Committee Chairman Kent Conrad described the agreement as a significant achievement. He said it advances Obama’s objectives of decreasing reliance on overseas energy, improving education, overhauling health care and providing tax relief to middle-class Americans.

The deal emerged as congressional negotiators worked to resolve differences between the separate House and Senate budget plans. Obama’s budget request totals $3.67 trillion.

Negotiators have accelerated one portion of the budget procedure. That move makes passage of a major health care overhaul this year more likely because Democrats can use a special mechanism called budget reconciliation. Under that process, Republicans would be unable to block the measure through the filibuster that had been broadly anticipated.

Democrats currently hold 58 Senate seats, so reconciliation would allow them to approve the legislation with a simple majority rather than the 60 votes required to defeat a filibuster.

Meanwhile, conservative House Democrats who have pressed party leaders to include a firm commitment to fiscal discipline may see some of their concerns addressed. A Democratic aide told CNN that House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and House Majority Whip Steny Hoyer were preparing a letter to Senate leaders that would forcefully demand adherence to a pay-as-you-go policy.

Under that system, any new federal expenditure would have to be balanced by spending reductions or higher taxes. Obama also urged Congress to adopt the legislation, commonly called “PAYGO,” during his weekend radio address.

Conrad said the budget resolution would hold growth in non-defense discretionary spending to 2.9 percent through 2014. He also said the plan would take meaningful short-term action by reducing the deficit by half by 2012 and by two-thirds by 2014. However, he cautioned that additional measures would be necessary to confront the country’s longer-term fiscal imbalance after the five-year budget period.

The previous week, Obama assembled his Cabinet and instructed its members to identify a combined $100 million in savings within 90 days.

Critics argued that $100 million is extremely small compared with the overall federal budget. One analogy likened it to a car dealership cutting just $1 from the price of a $36,700 automobile.

At the time, Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, a Kentucky Republican, said that any savings were welcome but noted that $100 million was roughly equal to the amount the government would spend each day merely paying interest on the stimulus package approved earlier in the year.

White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs responded that Americans outside Washington would still value the attempt to save money. He said that only in Washington would $100 million be considered insignificant, adding that it was a substantial sum where he came from and grew up, as well as for hundreds of millions of Americans.

CNN’s Deirdre Walsh contributed to the report.

The compromise provided a broad framework for federal spending, revenue, and deficit reduction while supporting the administration’s agenda on energy, education, health care, and tax policy.

President Barack Obama had requested a $3.67 trillion budget aimed at promoting energy independence, strengthening education, reforming the health care system, and providing tax relief for middle-class families. Although the congressional agreement did not necessarily adopt every element of the president’s proposal, it preserved many of its main objectives.

The House and Senate were expected to vote on the budget resolution during the week, potentially as early as Tuesday. Approval by both chambers would allow Congress to move forward with subsequent tax and spending legislation based on the agreed-upon fiscal framework.

A particularly significant feature of the agreement was the planned use of budget reconciliation to advance major health care reform. Reconciliation legislation can pass the Senate with a simple majority and is not subject to the usual 60-vote threshold needed to overcome a filibuster. This approach would therefore prevent Senate Republicans from blocking eligible portions of the health care package through extended debate.

At the same time, Democratic leaders sought to include safeguards intended to demonstrate fiscal discipline. These measures included pay-as-you-go, or PAYGO, rules requiring new spending or tax cuts to be offset by savings or additional revenue. The agreement also contemplated limits on increases in non-defense discretionary spending, balancing the administration’s policy ambitions with concerns about rising deficits.

House and Senate Democrats reached agreement on a fiscal 2010 budget framework built largely around President Barack Obama’s $3.67 trillion proposal. The compromise advances the administration’s major domestic priorities, including investments in renewable energy, education, health care, and middle-class tax relief, while also pledging to reduce the federal deficit over time.

The agreement reflects negotiations between the two chambers over spending levels, tax policy, and procedural rules. Although the congressional budget resolution does not itself appropriate money or change tax law, it establishes overall fiscal targets and creates a blueprint for subsequent legislation. Democratic leaders said the plan would support economic recovery while laying the groundwork for longer-term reforms.

A central feature of the agreement is its treatment of health care. The budget includes reconciliation instructions that could allow Congress to move health care legislation through the Senate under procedures requiring only a simple majority, rather than the 60 votes generally needed to overcome a filibuster. Democratic leaders described reconciliation as a fallback option intended to prevent a minority from blocking reform, while continuing to express a preference for developing a broader, bipartisan bill through the regular legislative process.

The reconciliation provision was important because Democrats remained divided over the cost and scope of health care reform. Liberal members wanted firm assurances that Congress would act, while some moderates and conservative Democrats were concerned about increasing the deficit or using an expedited procedure for such a significant policy change.

To address those fiscal concerns, negotiators also supported stronger pay-as-you-go requirements. Under proposed PAYGO rules, new tax cuts or mandatory spending increases would generally have to be offset by spending reductions or additional revenue elsewhere in the budget. Advocates said the rules would help restore discipline to the legislative process and demonstrate that new initiatives—including health care reform—would not simply be financed through additional borrowing.

The final agreement therefore sought to balance ambitious policy goals with demands for greater fiscal restraint. By combining investments in energy, education, health care, and tax relief with deficit-reduction targets and proposed PAYGO protections, Democratic leaders aimed to unite their caucus and advance the core elements of Obama’s economic agenda.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about House and Senate Democrats reaching an agreement on the fiscal 2010 budget resolution and its implications for Obama’s agenda.
counterfactuals.output:
# Democrats strike fiscal 2010 budget deal, advancing Obama agenda

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — House and Senate Democrats reached agreement Monday on a fiscal 2010 budget resolution that largely supports President Barack Obama’s domestic priorities and gives Congress a potential fast-track route for passing health care reform.

The roughly $3.4 trillion spending blueprint calls for major investments in health care, education and clean energy while seeking to reduce the federal deficit over five years. It does not carry the force of law or require the president’s signature, but it establishes spending and revenue targets that will guide congressional committees.

The compromise projects a deficit of about $1.2 trillion in fiscal 2010, down from the much larger shortfall expected in 2009, and aims to reduce the annual deficit to roughly $500 billion by 2014.

Democratic leaders said the agreement reflects Obama’s priorities while imposing tighter spending limits than those included in the president’s original budget proposal.

“This budget provides a framework for economic recovery and long-term growth,” Democrats said, arguing that it would allow Congress to address rising health costs, expand access to education and encourage development of alternative energy.

## Health care gets procedural boost

The most significant provision could be the inclusion of budget reconciliation instructions for health care and education legislation.

Reconciliation allows certain tax and spending measures to pass the Senate by a simple majority, limiting debate and preventing a filibuster. Democrats would otherwise need 60 votes to overcome Republican opposition or resistance from members of their own party.

Democratic leaders have said they hope to approve a bipartisan health care overhaul through the regular legislative process. But the reconciliation option gives them leverage — and a backup plan — if negotiations stall.

The agreement does not provide the same expedited protection for climate change legislation, reflecting concerns among moderate Democrats from industrial and energy-producing states about the cost of a proposed cap-and-trade system.

## Differences with Obama’s proposal

Congressional negotiators scaled back some elements of Obama’s initial plan, including portions of his proposed tax reductions and domestic spending increases.

The resolution assumes that tax cuts enacted under President George W. Bush will be extended for most households but allowed to expire for higher-income taxpayers. It also leaves room for changes to the estate tax and other provisions that remained under debate.

As a budget resolution, the measure does not itself raise taxes, cut specific programs or create a health care system. Those decisions would have to be made in separate legislation.

Republicans criticized the agreement as a blueprint for higher spending, larger government and increased taxes. They also objected to the possible use of reconciliation for health care, saying such a major policy change should require broader support.

Democrats countered that the budget inherited a severe recession, costly wars and a rapidly growing deficit, making short-term spending necessary to stabilize the economy.

The agreement must still win final approval in both chambers. Democratic majorities are expected to provide enough votes, despite little or no Republican support.

If adopted, the resolution would mark an important early victory for Obama by giving lawmakers a framework to pursue the central promises of his first-year agenda — particularly health care reform — while beginning a longer-term debate over taxes, spending and the federal debt.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the 2009 congressional budget negotiations, including the $3.67 trillion Obama budget request, health care reconciliation, PAYGO rules, and proposed spending cuts.
counterfactuals.output:
## Report: 2009 Congressional Budget Negotiations

### Overview

The 2009 budget debate took place amid the deepest phase of the Great Recession, shortly after enactment of the $787 billion American Recovery and Reinvestment Act. President Barack Obama’s first budget sought to combine short-term economic support with major initiatives in health care, energy, education, and financial regulation.

The administration’s fiscal year 2010 request was commonly described at the time as approximately **$3.6 trillion to $3.67 trillion**, depending on the budget table and treatment of certain programs. It projected an extraordinarily large fiscal year 2009 deficit—about **$1.75 trillion**—followed by a still-large deficit of roughly **$1.2 trillion in 2010**.

Congressional Democrats broadly supported Obama’s priorities but reduced some spending assumptions, declined to endorse every proposed tax or policy change, and sought procedural tools to advance health reform. Republicans opposed the plan almost unanimously, arguing that it relied on excessive spending, taxation, and borrowing.

### House and Senate negotiations

The House and Senate passed separate budget resolutions in early April 2009. Both were below the administration’s headline request and made different assumptions about discretionary spending, taxes, and future deficits.

Key negotiating issues included:

- How much of Obama’s proposed domestic agenda could be accommodated while deficits were rising sharply.
- Whether the budget should assume extension of tax relief for households earning below approximately $250,000.
- How to create room for health-care reform without formally approving a specific bill.
- Whether to use the reconciliation process, which would limit the Senate’s ability to filibuster budget-related legislation.
- How strictly Congress should apply “pay-as-you-go,” or PAYGO, requirements.
- The amount of defense and nondefense discretionary spending.

The final conference agreement, **S. Con. Res. 13**, was approved on April 29, 2009, by votes of **233–193 in the House** and **53–43 in the Senate**. The congressional plan was generally described as roughly a **$3.4 trillion fiscal year 2010 budget**, smaller than the administration’s request but still supportive of its central policy goals.

A congressional budget resolution does not itself appropriate money or change tax law. It establishes spending and revenue targets and provides procedural instructions for later legislation.

### Health care and reconciliation

The most consequential procedural dispute concerned health-care reform. Democratic leaders wanted to preserve the option of using **budget reconciliation** if bipartisan negotiations stalled.

Reconciliation legislation is protected from a Senate filibuster and can pass with a simple majority, but its provisions must have a genuine budgetary effect and remain subject to the Senate’s “Byrd Rule,” which can exclude provisions considered merely incidental to spending or revenue.

The final budget resolution:

- Created room for deficit-neutral health-care legislation.
- Directed relevant House and Senate committees to produce legislation achieving at least nominal deficit reduction.
- Set an October 15, 2009, timetable for committee action.
- Preserved reconciliation as a fallback rather than requiring that the entire health-care bill immediately be written through that process.

This did not mean that all health-care policy could automatically be enacted with 51 Senate votes. In the end, the main Affordable Care Act passed the Senate in December 2009 under regular procedures after Democrats overcame a filibuster. A separate reconciliation measure was used in March 2010 to modify taxes, subsidies, Medicare provisions, and other budget-related portions of the law.

### PAYGO rules

PAYGO was another major part of the debate. Under pay-as-you-go principles, new mandatory spending or tax reductions had to be offset by spending cuts or revenue increases elsewhere so that they would not add to the deficit.

Congress already operated under internal PAYGO rules, but enforcement and exceptions were contested. Democrats argued that PAYGO would impose discipline on new long-term initiatives, particularly health reform. Republicans countered that the budget tolerated large deficits and that exemptions undermined the rule.

The Obama administration also advocated restoring **statutory PAYGO**, under which violations could eventually trigger automatic spending reductions. Its proposal contemplated special treatment for several policies regarded as continuations of existing practice, including:

- Extension of middle-class portions of the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts.
- Annual adjustments to prevent the alternative minimum tax from affecting more taxpayers.
- Changes preventing scheduled cuts in Medicare physician payments.
- Certain estate-tax policies.

The House passed statutory PAYGO legislation in 2009; a version was ultimately enacted in February 2010. In the 2009 negotiations themselves, PAYGO mainly functioned as a budget-enforcement principle and as the basis for requiring health legislation to be deficit-neutral.

### Proposed spending cuts and savings

Although the budget expanded federal activity in several areas, the administration and congressional negotiators also proposed reductions. The largest proposed savings generally came from restructuring existing programs rather than broad across-the-board cuts.

Major proposals included:

- **Health programs:** Reducing payments to private Medicare Advantage plans and pursuing other Medicare and Medicaid efficiencies to help finance health reform.
- **Defense procurement:** Ending or scaling back systems such as further F-22 fighter production, the VH-71 presidential helicopter, and parts of the Army’s Future Combat Systems program.
- **Agriculture:** Restricting farm payments to higher-income recipients and reducing certain agricultural subsidies.
- **Student lending:** Ending subsidies to private lenders under the guaranteed student-loan system and moving toward direct federal lending.
- **Program eliminations and reductions:** The administration later identified approximately **121 programs** for termination or reduction, claiming about **$17 billion in fiscal year 2010 savings**.
- **Administrative economies:** Obama also ordered agencies to identify $100 million in administrative savings. The initiative attracted criticism because the amount was extremely small relative to a multitrillion-dollar budget.

Many proposed cuts faced resistance from members of Congress whose states or districts benefited from the affected programs. As a result, not all administration proposals were incorporated into appropriations or authorizing legislation.

### Outcome and significance

The 2009 congressional budget largely ratified Obama’s broad agenda while imposing somewhat lower spending levels and retaining congressional discretion over the details. Its most important immediate effects were procedural:

1. It established fiscal targets for subsequent appropriations and tax legislation.
2. It created budgetary space for health-care reform.
3. It preserved reconciliation as a means of advancing budget-related health provisions.
4. It reaffirmed PAYGO as the governing principle for new entitlement expansions and tax cuts.
5. It signaled support for selected spending reductions, though Congress later modified or rejected many individual cuts.

The negotiations also exposed a lasting tension in the administration’s fiscal strategy: Obama sought to address long-term costs and eliminate selected inefficient programs while simultaneously using substantial federal spending and tax incentives to combat the recession and launch major policy initiatives.

**BREAKING: Democrats Reach Deal on $3.4 Trillion Federal Budget**

**WASHINGTON, April 27, 2009** — Democratic negotiators in Congress reached agreement Monday on a fiscal 2010 budget blueprint that advances President Barack Obama’s domestic agenda while setting up battles over health care, taxes and federal spending.

“We have reached an agreement on a budget resolution,” Senate Budget Committee Chairman Kent Conrad, D-N.D., said as House and Senate negotiators completed work on the plan.

The roughly $3.4 trillion measure would provide room for Obama’s priorities in health care, education and energy while projecting a lower deficit over several years. The nonbinding resolution does not appropriate money, but it establishes spending and revenue targets that will guide lawmakers as they draft tax and spending legislation.

The agreement also includes a procedural option that could allow Democrats to move health-care legislation through the Senate with a simple majority, limiting Republicans’ ability to block it with a filibuster.

Republicans sharply criticized the plan. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., said it “spends too much, taxes too much and borrows too much,” arguing that Democrats were adding to the national debt during a severe recession.

The White House welcomed the agreement. Press secretary Robert Gibbs said, “The president is pleased that the House and Senate have come to an agreement on a budget that lays the foundation for his agenda.”

Final votes in both chambers are expected later this week. Democrats hold majorities in the House and Senate, and the budget can pass without Republican support.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how the fiscal 2010 budget agreement could help Democrats pass health care reform without a Republican filibuster, while also addressing concerns about fiscal responsibility.
counterfactuals.output:
The fiscal 2010 budget agreement gave Democrats a **reconciliation fallback** for health care reform. It instructed key House and Senate committees to produce legislation reducing the deficit, potentially including health care provisions.

Reconciliation mattered because, in the Senate:

- debate is limited;
- amendments face special restrictions; and
- the bill can pass with a simple majority—normally 51 votes—rather than the 60 votes needed to overcome a Republican filibuster.

Thus, Democrats could first seek a bipartisan bill through normal procedures but use reconciliation if Republicans blocked it.

The agreement also addressed fiscal-responsibility concerns by requiring the legislation to be **deficit-neutral or deficit-reducing**, with new spending offset by Medicare or other health-system savings, spending cuts, or added revenue. Reconciliation rules—especially the Byrd Rule—also make it difficult to include provisions that are merely policy changes with little budgetary effect or that increase deficits beyond the budget window.

So the budget agreement paired a filibuster-proof route with fiscal constraints, although reconciliation could not easily carry every nonbudgetary element of a comprehensive health reform bill.

# House and Senate negotiators strike budget deal, narrowing Obama’s spending plans

**WASHINGTON** — House and Senate negotiators reached agreement on a roughly **$3.5 trillion fiscal 2010 budget framework**, giving President Barack Obama a significant early legislative victory while trimming some of his domestic spending ambitions and setting targets for reducing the federal deficit.

The congressional budget resolution is not a law and does not appropriate money. Instead, it establishes spending and revenue guidelines for later tax and appropriations legislation. The compromise broadly supports Obama’s agenda on health care, education and energy, but reflects concerns among moderate Democrats about rapidly rising deficits.

## Non-defense discretionary spending trimmed

The agreement allows non-defense discretionary spending — funding for domestic agencies and programs outside entitlement programs such as Social Security and Medicare — to increase substantially over the previous year.

However, congressional negotiators set the total below the level requested by the White House. Obama had proposed an increase of roughly **9%**, while the final congressional framework was closer to **7%**, depending on the baseline and which emergency funds were included.

That meant billions of dollars less for domestic programs than the administration initially sought. Democratic leaders nevertheless argued that the budget preserved the president’s central priorities, including investments in health care reform, education, clean energy and infrastructure.

Defense and national-security spending remained largely protected, although the budget framework left the precise allocation of funds to the annual appropriations process.

## Deficit remains high but is projected to decline

The deal projected a federal deficit of approximately **$1.2 trillion in fiscal 2010**, following an even larger shortfall during the recession and the government’s response to the financial crisis.

Under the congressional plan, the deficit would gradually fall to about **$500 billion to $525 billion by fiscal 2014**. That would represent a substantial reduction in dollar terms, although the government would continue borrowing heavily and adding to the national debt.

Democrats emphasized that the deficit was expected to decline as the economy recovered and temporary stimulus and financial-rescue costs expired. Republicans countered that the plan still envisioned years of historically large deficits and did not do enough to restrain entitlement spending.

The targets also depended on economic assumptions, future congressional action and the expectation that some of Obama’s policy initiatives would either be paid for or produce long-term savings.

## Obama’s $100 million savings initiative

The budget negotiations unfolded as Obama directed his Cabinet to identify **$100 million in administrative savings** over 90 days. The White House presented the initiative as part of a broader effort to eliminate waste and demonstrate fiscal discipline.

Officials cited possible savings from reducing travel, consolidating purchases, cutting unnecessary printing and publications, and improving government procurement.

The initiative drew immediate skepticism because of its scale. In a federal budget measured in trillions of dollars, $100 million represented only a tiny fraction of annual spending and was negligible compared with deficits exceeding $1 trillion.

The administration acknowledged that the amount would not materially alter the deficit. Obama argued instead that the effort was intended to change the culture of government and show taxpayers that agencies were being asked to scrutinize even relatively small expenses.

Critics, particularly congressional Republicans, called the announcement symbolic and said meaningful deficit reduction would require larger changes to domestic programs, taxes and major entitlement systems.

## Democratic leaders claim progress

House Speaker **Nancy Pelosi** and Senate Majority Leader **Harry Reid** welcomed the agreement as a responsible framework that balanced economic investment with deficit reduction.

Democratic leaders said the plan advanced Obama’s priorities while making adjustments demanded by lawmakers concerned about spending. They also stressed that the budget would allow Congress to begin work on health care reform and other major legislation.

A particularly important element was the possibility of using the **budget reconciliation process** for health care. Reconciliation legislation can pass the Senate with a simple majority and cannot be blocked by a filibuster, though its provisions must have a direct budgetary effect.

Democrats described reconciliation as a fallback rather than their preferred route, saying they still hoped to produce bipartisan health care legislation. Republicans said its inclusion showed Democrats were preparing to force through a sweeping overhaul without broad support.

## Republicans attack spending and debt

Republican congressional leaders rejected the compromise, arguing that it spent too much, borrowed too much and could lead to higher taxes.

They said the projected decline in the annual deficit did not change the fact that the government would continue accumulating trillions of dollars in new debt. Republicans also criticized Democratic assumptions about future economic growth and savings from health care reform.

GOP lawmakers linked the budget agreement to Obama’s $100 million savings directive, arguing that small administrative cuts could not offset the administration’s broader expansion of federal spending.

## Political significance

The compromise demonstrated that Obama retained strong support among congressional Democrats, but it also revealed limits to that support. Moderate and fiscally conservative Democrats pushed the administration to accept lower domestic spending levels and clearer deficit-reduction goals.

Because the resolution did not require the president’s signature, its immediate importance was procedural and political. It provided Congress with a blueprint for subsequent spending and tax bills and created a possible path for advancing health care reform.

The deal therefore represented both an endorsement and a restraint: Democrats embraced much of Obama’s domestic agenda, but they also signaled that concerns about deficits would shape how quickly — and how fully — that agenda could be enacted.
